# Part 1 — Reconstruct the Data 

**Variables Used**

B17001_001E : total population for whom poverty status is determined - This will be used to determine the poverty rate. Using "B01003_001E : total population" would not be accurate because the ACS excludes some people from their poverty rate calculation if they are determined inapplicable. 

B17001_002E : total population below the poverty level - This will be used to determine the poverty rate. Dividing the total population below the poverty level by the total population applicable will give me the poverty rate. 

B17001_001M : MOE for the total - The margin of error will allow me to determine the certainity of the statistical outcome.

B17001_002M : MOE for below poverty - The margin of error will allow me to determine the certainty of the statistical outcome. 

I used the 2006-2010 ACS5 survey data to represent the 2010 data mentioned in the article, and the 2013-2017 ACS5 survey data to represent the 2017 data mentioned in the article. Although the article mentions some data from the 2016 ACS1 report, it's main claim compares the change in the poverty rate from 2010 to 2017. The two periods do not overlap.  

I assumed that the article correctly calculated the poverty rate by using "total population for whom poverty status is determined" rather than just "total population". I myself did not realize that this is the correct way to calculate the poverty rate before reading this on the US Census Bureau website.

# Part 2 — Test (code plus interpretation)


**Data Setup**
```{r}
#| label: setup
library (tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(gt)
```

```{r}
vars <- c(
total = "B17001_001",
below = "B17001_002"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output ="wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)
```


**Compute the Poverty Rate**
```{r}
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_rt = belowE / totalE)
acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_rt = belowE / totalE)
```

**Compute the Margin of Error (MOE)**
```{r}
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_moe = moe_prop(
  belowE,
  totalE,
  belowM,
  totalM
))

acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_moe = moe_prop(
  belowE,
  totalE,
  belowM,
  totalM
))
```

**Compute the coefficient of variation**
```{r}
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_cv = ((poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rt) * 100)
acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_cv = ((poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rt) * 100)
```

**Flag reliability using the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.**
```{r}
reliability_table_2010 <- acs_2010 |> 
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ "",
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ "Not available",
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(poverty_cv)) |> 
  select(
    dot,
    NAME,
    totalE,
    belowE,
    poverty_rt,
    poverty_moe,
    poverty_cv,
    flag
  )

reliability_table_2010 |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(totalE, belowE),
    decimals = 0
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_rt,
    decimals = 1,
    scale_by = 100
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_moe,
    decimals = 3
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_cv,
    decimals = 1
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Census Tract",
    totalE = "Population",
    belowE = "Below Poverty",
    poverty_rt = "Poverty Rate (%)",
    poverty_moe = "MOE",
    poverty_cv = "CV (%)",
    flag = "Reliability"
  ) |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = dot
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Reliability of Philadelphia Census Tract Poverty Rates",
    subtitle = "ACS 2006–2010 5-year estimates"
  ) |> 
  tab_source_note(
    "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable."
  )
reliability_table_2017 <- acs_2017 |> 
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ "",
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ "Not available",
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(poverty_cv)) |> 
  select(
    dot,
    NAME,
    totalE,
    belowE,
    poverty_rt,
    poverty_moe,
    poverty_cv,
    flag
  )

reliability_table_2017 |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(totalE, belowE),
    decimals = 0
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_rt,
    decimals = 1,
    scale_by = 100
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_moe,
    decimals = 3
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_cv,
    decimals = 1
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Census Tract",
    totalE = "Population",
    belowE = "Below Poverty",
    poverty_rt = "Poverty Rate (%)",
    poverty_moe = "MOE",
    poverty_cv = "CV (%)",
    flag = "Reliability"
  ) |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = dot
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Reliability of Philadelphia Census Tract Poverty Rates",
    subtitle = "ACS 2013–2017 5-year estimates"
  ) |>

    "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable."
  )
 
reliability_table_2010
reliability_table_2017
```

  
**Compute the change between the two periods and the margin of error of that change.**
```{r}
poverty_change <- acs_2010 |> 
  select(GEOID, NAME, poverty_rt_2010 = poverty_rt, poverty_moe_2010 = poverty_moe) |> 
  left_join( acs_2017 |> 
  select(GEOID, poverty_rt_2017 = poverty_rt, poverty_moe_2017 = poverty_moe),
  by = "GEOID")
  
poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
  mutate(poverty_change = poverty_rt_2017 - poverty_rt_2010)
  
poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
mutate(
  se_2010 = poverty_moe_2010 / 1.645,
  se_2017 = poverty_moe_2017 / 1.645,
  se_change = sqrt(se_2010^2 + se_2017^2),
  change_moe = 1.645 * se_change
)
  
head(poverty_change)
```


# FIGURE 1: Distribution of Poverty Rates: 2010 vs. 2017
```{r}
#| label: fig-poverty-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Philadelphia census tract pov"
poverty_long <- poverty_change |>
  select(
    GEOID,
    poverty_rt_2010,
    poverty_rt_2017
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(poverty_rt_2010, poverty_rt_2017),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "poverty_rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = recode(
      year,
      poverty_rt_2010 = "2010",
      poverty_rt_2017 = "2017"
    ),
    poverty_rate = poverty_rate * 100
  )
figure_1 <- ggplot(
  poverty_long,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = poverty_rate,
    fill = year
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.75,
    width = 0.6,
    outlier.alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Philadelphia Census Tract Poverty Rates",
    subtitle = "Comparison of ACS 5-Year estimates for 2010 and 2017",
    x = "Period",
    y = "Poverty rate (%)",
    fill = "Period",
    caption = paste(
      "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-Year Estimates.",
      "Poverty rate = population below poverty level /",
      "population for whom poverty status is determined."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

figure_1
```

# FIGURE 2: Change in poverty rate with 90% margin of error
```{r}
#| label: fig-poverty-change
#| fig-cap: "Change in Philadelphia census tract poverty r"
error_bar_data <- poverty_change |>
  filter(
    !is.na(poverty_change),
    !is.na(change_moe)
  ) |>
  arrange(poverty_change) |>
  mutate(
    tract_order = row_number()
  )
figure_2 <- ggplot(
  error_bar_data,
  aes(
    x = tract_order,
    y = poverty_change * 100
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = (poverty_change - change_moe) * 100,
      ymax = (poverty_change + change_moe) * 100
    ),
    width = 0,
    alpha = 0.35,
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.7,
    color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in Poverty Rates Across Philadelphia Census Tracts",
    subtitle = "2017 minus 2010 poverty rate; points show estimates and bars show 90% margins of error",
    x = "Philadelphia census tracts, ordered by estimated change",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-Year Estimates (2006–2010 and 2013–2017)."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

figure_2
```

**Is change statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence?**
```{r}
poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
  mutate(
  lower = poverty_change - change_moe,
  upper = poverty_change + change_moe,
  significant_90 = lower > 0 | upper < 0
)
```

**How many tracts show a statistically detectable change and how many do not?**
```{r}
table(poverty_change$significant_90)
```

FALSE: 313
There are 313 tracts without statistically detectable change.

TRUE: 63
There are 63 tracts with statistically detectable change. 

**What tracts have missing values?**
```{r}
poverty_change |> 
  filter(is.na(significant_90)) |> 
  select(GEOID, NAME)
```

These tracts have missing values: 
50 : Philadelphia Navy Yard
9803 : NA
9804 : Philadelphia International Airport
9805 : NA
9806 : Stadiums / Commercial Area
9807 : Stadiums / Commercial Area
9808 : NA
9809 : Philadelphia International Airport

# Part 3 — Adjudicate

The analysis supports the article's claim that that poverty rates changed in some Philadelphia census tracts between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS periods. 

That being said, this analysis cannot be used to determine a large majority of the claims in the article. This is for a variety of reasons but mainly being that the data only represents the poverty rate and does not indicate other factors such as the depth of poverty, the race associated with each tract, or the reason for which an individual may be in poverty. For this reason, claims such as 50% or more of people in poverty are living below the federal poverty rate, and a lack of employment, drug addiction, immigration or retirement are the main causes for increased poverty rates, cannot be supported. 

Additionally, the article details poverty at the neighborhood scale whereas the census collects data by tracts, thus also making it difficult to draw sound data-based conclusions. Claims such as certain neighborhoods are becoming destinations for impoverished households to move into and poverty rates in majority-white neighborhoods are dramatically increasing cannot be fully determined since a single neighborhood is typically comprised of multiple tracts. Furthermore, census tracts do not fit neatly into a neighborhood boundary (which itself is up for dispute), but rather can cross and cut through neighborhoods in a variety of ways. 

Finally, most of the claims in the article are anecdotal. Although they are presented alongside the census data and by seemingly reputable sources - food pantry directors, community organizers, social workers, etc. - this does not mean that the census data directly supports these claims.

In general, the ACS data supports evidence of change in some tracts, but not the causal explanations offered for why those changes occurred.

---

# Part 4 — Rewrite 

**A new five-year federal survey shows that poverty rates changed in some Philadelphia neighborhoods between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 periods. In my analysis, 63 of 376 tracts had poverty-rate changes that were statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90 percent confidence level, while 313 did not. The data therefore shows that poverty shifted significantly in some parts of the city, but not all of it. It also does not establish why those changes occurred. The survey cannot determine whether changes resulted from the Great Recession, unemployment, migration, evictions, opioid addiction, retirement, or other factors suggested by residents and community leaders. Those explanations require additional evidence beyond the ACS poverty estimates. The five-year ACS also carries margins of error, making it important to distinguish measurable changes from differences that may reflect sampling uncertainty.**
